The nightingale, as soon as April bringeth Unto her rested sense a perfect waking, While late bare earth, proud of new clothing, springeth, Sings out her woes, a thorn her song-book making, And mournfully bewailing, Her throat in tunes expresseth What grief her breast oppresseth For Tereus’ force on her chaste will prevailing. # The Nightingale's Lament and the Speaker's Deeper Wound

Each April, as the natural world stirs from its winter slumber, the nightingale lifts her voice in song—a song that, according to ancient tradition, is not one of pure joy but of enduring mourning. This is Philomela, the mythological figure transformed into the nightingale after suffering a brutal violation at the hands of Tereus, her sister's husband. In the myth, Tereus not only assaulted her but cut out her tongue to silence her, leaving her to weave her story into a tapestry since she could no longer speak it. Now, as a bird, she finds a different instrument for her testimony: a thorn pressed against her breast, said to be the source of her plaintive song. This thorn becomes her book, her only means of recording and releasing the ancient trauma that still echoes through her yearly cry.

The speaker of the poem observes this seasonal ritual with a complicated mixture of sympathy and self-reflection. All around him, spring performs its usual miracle—the earth softens, greenery erupts, life renews itself in the customary rhythm of the seasons. Yet this annual rebirth, which seems to offer the nightingale at least a temporary stage for her grief, finds no parallel in the speaker's own heart. His desolation is not seasonal; it does not wax and wane with the turning of the calendar. While the world around him bursts into color and vitality, his inner landscape remains barren, untouched by the same regenerative promise that spring extends to every other living thing.

Here the speaker draws a crucial distinction between his suffering and Philomela's. Her anguish, however profound and however eternally commemorated in song, stems from a single historical event—a violation that, however horrific, has already occurred and now exists only in memory and ritual reenactment. Her wound, though deep, is a wound of the past: completed, finished, sealed into the permanent record of what was done to her against her will. The speaker's affliction operates on an entirely different register. His suffering is not the echo of a past injury but the constant, grinding presence of an unfulfilled desire—a longing that has no terminus, no moment of completion, no closure. Where Philomela mourns what was taken from her, the speaker suffers from what he has never been permitted to have.

From this distinction, the speaker advances a bold and perhaps startling claim: that his pain, in fact, surpasses hers in severity. He argues that there exists a meaningful difference between suffering a singular, if terrible, wrong and enduring the perpetual ache of unsatisfied want. Philomela's grief, though rooted in violence, at least possesses the shape of a completed narrative—an act that happened once and can be mourned, sung, and in some sense processed through ritual repetition. The speaker's condition offers no such resolution. His desire persists without end, a wound that never closes because it was never inflicted all at once but instead continuously reopens with each passing day of longing. In this framing, perpetual unfulfilled desire becomes, paradoxically, a deeper and more corrosive form of suffering than even the trauma of violation—for at least violation, however unjust, reaches an end, while longing that is perpetually denied has no such mercy.

This argument crystallizes in the poem's refrain, which returns again and again to address Philomela directly, urging her toward some measure of comfort or consolation. The speaker's message to her is consistent: though her thorn is real, sharp, and historically justified as an emblem of her suffering, it is nonetheless an external thing—a physical, visible mark of pain that she can point to and articulate through song. His own thorn, by contrast, is hidden, internal, and born not of a single violent act but of the unrelenting presence of desire that finds no fulfillment. Each time the refrain returns, it reinforces this central paradox: that the invisible, ongoing thorn of longing pierces more deeply than the visible, storied thorn of past violation, and that the speaker, despite lacking Philomela's mythic gravitas, bears a burden that in its way exceeds even hers.
outputs.L4:
# The Nightingale's Complaint and the Deeper Wound of Desire

Sir Philip Sidney's poem "The Nightingale" opens with the arrival of spring, a season traditionally associated with renewal, fertility, and joy. Yet Sidney immediately complicates this expectation by turning to the nightingale—Philomela in classical mythology—whose song, far from being a simple celebration of the season, is transformed into an annual ritual of mourning. As the earth "springeth" with new growth and "proud of new clothing," the nightingale's voice rises not in harmony with this renewal but in stark contrast to it, retelling through her music the ancient violation she suffered at the hands of Tereus.

The mythological backdrop is essential to understanding the poem's emotional architecture. In the story inherited from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Philomela was raped by Tereus, her brother-in-law, who then cut out her tongue to silence her. Through the intervention of the gods, she was transformed into a nightingale, and her song became eternally bound to the memory of that violence—a "thorn" pressed against her breast as she sings, according to the old poetic convention that the nightingale sings against a thorn to keep herself awake and mournful. Her annual lament, then, is a form of ritualized grief: fixed, patterned, and directed at a specific, completed wrong. Her suffering, however profound, has a clear origin and a defined shape. It is grief *for something that happened*.

Sidney's speaker, listening to this song, might be expected to find in it a mirror for his own sorrow, or even a source of sympathy. Instead, he makes a startling move: he addresses Philomela directly and tells her, in effect, that she has less reason for sorrow than he does. "O Philomela fair," he says, "take some gladness"—not because her pain is illegitimate, but because his own is greater. Where her world is one of springing earth and external thorns, his internal landscape is barren, and his own metaphorical thorn pierces not a resting breast from outside but invades his heart from within.

The crux of the poem's argument, and its most striking paradox, comes in the comparison between Philomela's completed violation and the speaker's unresolved, ongoing desire. Philomela's anguish, Sidney's speaker insists, stems from a single, historical act of force—terrible, but finished. She "suffering, all her spirits languish" over what was done to her once, however permanently that act altered her fate. The speaker's condition, by contrast, is a state of perpetual, unsatisfied craving: he desires daily and daily fails to attain what he desires. There is no discrete event to mourn and move past, only an unending present tense of lack.

This leads to the poem's central declaration, one of the more psychologically acute claims in Renaissance love poetry: "wanting is more woe than too much having." The line inverts what might seem like intuitive moral and emotional logic—surely a violation, a "too much having" imposed by force upon an unwilling victim, would constitute the greater suffering. Yet Sidney's speaker argues that the torment of frustrated desire, precisely because it is never resolved, never allowed to become memory or history, is in fact more corrosive to the spirit. Philomela's wound, though horrific, is sealed into the past; she can, in some sense, complete her grief through the ritual of song. The speaker's wound, by contrast, remains perpetually open, renewed each day by continued craving that finds no satisfaction.

This paradox illuminates a broader theme running through the poem: the peculiar cruelty of unfulfilled longing as compared to accomplished violation or loss. There is, embedded in this argument, a meditation on the nature of desire itself—the idea that the mind's endless reaching toward an unattained object may generate a more sustained and gnawing anguish than even a severe, completed injury. Completed wrongs, however terrible, can become fixed points around which grief organizes itself, eventually taking narrative and even musical form, as Philomela's grief does. Unfulfilled desire, however, resists this kind of resolution; it has no ending, no story to tell, only repetition without release.

By setting his own suffering against the mythic and seemingly definitive tragedy of Philomela, Sidney's speaker makes a bold and somewhat unsettling claim about the hierarchy of emotional pain, elevating the private, ongoing torment of thwarted desire above even the archetypal suffering of sexual violation preserved in classical myth. The poem thus becomes not merely a lament of unrequited love but a meditation on the peculiar psychological weight of "wanting" itself—suggesting that the absence of resolution, the perpetual reaching without arrival, constitutes its own distinct and perhaps more insidious form of suffering.
outputs.L5:
# The Arrival of April

The month of April carries with it a particular kind of magic—the quiet unfolding of life after winter's long silence. There is something almost sacred in watching the first green shoots push through soil that seemed, only weeks before, incapable of sustaining anything at all.

Unto this season we entrust our hopes for renewal. Unto the lengthening days we offer our patience, worn thin by months of gray skies and early darkness. The rains of April, though sometimes relentless, serve a purpose beyond mere inconvenience; they awaken roots that have slept, coaxing forth blossoms that will, in time, become the fruit of summer.

There is an old rhythm to this transition, one that predates calendars and clocks. Farmers have long understood April as a threshold month—neither the harshness of winter nor the abundance of summer, but something in between. A promise, perhaps, more than a fulfillment.

The birds seem to sense it first. Their return marks the unofficial start of the season, their songs filling mornings that had been silent for too long. Children venture outside without heavy coats. The scent of wet earth mingles with the first hints of blooming flowers.

Unto each of us, April offers a kind of invitation: to shed what no longer serves us, to make room for growth, to trust that what feels uncertain now will, given time, become something beautiful. The month asks for patience and rewards it in equal measure—a fair exchange, if ever there was one.

In this way, April becomes more than a name on a calendar. It becomes a metaphor for all the small rebirths we experience throughout our lives, reminding us that even after the coldest seasons, warmth returns.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Renaissance-style double sestina-inspired lyric about a nightingale mourning like Philomela, using archaic English diction.
counterfactuals.output:
*On the double sestina and its scale:* the true double sestina — twelve stanzas of twelve lines, as Sidney wrought in "Ye Goatherd Gods" — is among the most demanding architectures in English verse, its six governing words wheeling through 144 lines before resolving in a final envoi. In that spirit, and at a scale that honors the form's obsessive, circling grief without diluting its precision, here is a single sestina (the double sestina's root form) built on six words — **night, plaint, thorn, grief, song, wood** — mourning after the manner of Philomela.

---

**The Nightingale's Complaint**

Whenas the sun forsakes the weeping night,
the nightingale begins her ancient plaint,
and presses her soft breast upon the thorn,
that inward smart may waken outward grief,
and from her ravished tongue there flows a song
so sweet, so sad, it fills the shuddering wood.

O Philomel, whom cruel Tereus' wood
and lawless lust did hunt through pathless night,
thy tongue was reft, yet heaven gave thee song;
now every leaf doth learn thy piteous plaint,
and every bird grows silent at thy grief,
as if the world were made one living thorn.

She sings as one who loves the piercing thorn,
for sweeter is the pain than sleep i' the wood;
she calls to Tereus through the vault of night,
and Procne answers with a sister's grief;
between them flies the shuttle of their plaint,
enwoven with the fatal thread of song.

Ah, hapless bird, whose only art is song,
whose only bed henceforth shall be the thorn,
teach me, poor swain, the science of thy plaint,
that I may mourn as thou dost in the wood
my love, that like a rose did bloom by night
and perished ere the morning knew her grief.

Methinks the stars grow pale to hear such grief,
methinks the moon doth stay to hear thy song,
for never yet did any child of night
lay down her body on so sharp a thorn;
yet still she sings, as I sing in this wood,
and still the world is deaf unto our plaint.

Then let us twain make one continual plaint,
one antique music of undying grief,
till echo learn it through the hollow wood,
till shepherds weep to hear so true a song,
till time itself lie down upon the thorn
and die, as we shall die, into the night.

*Envoi*

Sing, Philomel, thy thorn-taught, deathless song;
let night receive our grief, our ancient plaint;
so ends the tale the wood doth tell, and moan.
